{
  "research_question": "How does mouse navigation performance vary across different stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham) when assessed by time to target, success rate, path efficiency, average speed, and angular dispersion?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "The dataset contains 76655 trials across 8 mice after filtering for the five specified stimulation paradigms.",
    "Combined stimulation is the most frequent paradigm with 48846 trials (63.7%), followed by ICMS Only (11378 trials, 14.9%), Dim Visual Only (9603 trials, 12.6%), Sham (3505 trials, 4.6%), and Bright Visual Only (3323 trials, 4.3%).",
    "Overall success rate across all paradigms is 72.95% (SD=0.444), with mean Time-to-Target of 2.81 seconds (SD=2.08).",
    "Mean path efficiency is 0.475 (SD=0.467), indicating substantial variability in directness of navigation paths.",
    "Average speed across trials is 12.50 units (SD=4.46), while angular dispersion (AD) averages 0.377 (SD=0.240)."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "Sample size imbalance across paradigms is extreme: Combined has ~15× more trials than Bright Visual Only and Sham, and ~5× more than Dim Visual Only and ICMS Only, limiting precision of between-paradigm comparisons.",
    "Overall Success rate of 73% suggests possible floor/ceiling effects that may differ by paradigm, but paradigm-specific success rates cannot be computed from summary_only data.",
    "Path efficiency shows high variance (SD nearly equal to mean, max=29.8) suggesting potential outliers or multi-modal distributions that may differ by paradigm.",
    "AD ranges from near-zero to 1.0 with substantial spread (SD=0.24), indicating some trials had highly variable heading directions while others were very directed; paradigm-specific patterns in this variability are unknown."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "Based solely on these marginal summaries, no definitive conclusions can be drawn about paradigm-specific effects. The dataset structure with highly unbalanced replication (Combined >> ICMS Only > Visual conditions > Sham) requires stratified analysis before inferring performance differences. The substantial variability in path efficiency and angular dispersion across all trials suggests that stimulation effects—if present—may interact with trial-specific factors like target location, initial heading, or motivational state that are not recoverable from summary statistics.",
  "limitations": [
    "data_view=summary_only provides only marginal distributions; no paradigm-specific means, variances, or effect sizes can be computed.",
    "Extreme sample size imbalance (63.7% Combined vs 4.3% Bright Visual Only) makes between-paradigm comparisons statistically unreliable without weighting or subsampling.",
    "Success is binary but only overall mean is provided; no information on paradigm-specific success rates or failure mode distributions.",
    "AD (angular dispersion) interpretation is uncertain: it could represent heading variability, directional error, or confidence measure, with different implications for each.",
    "No repeated-measures structure is preserved; individual mouse effects cannot be separated from paradigm effects.",
    "No temporal or learning effects can be assessed; all trials are pooled, potentially mixing early and late performance.",
    "Outliers exist (Path Efficiency max=29.8 vs mean=0.47) but their paradigm membership is unknown."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Request data_view=aggregated_by_paradigm or individual trial-level data to obtain paradigm-specific means and confidence intervals for all five response variables. If individual-level data is unavailable, a stratified bootstrap or weighted analysis accounting for the severe sample imbalance would be the minimum required step. Additionally, mixed-effects modeling with Mouse as random effect is recommended to properly estimate stimulation effects while accounting for individual differences and repeated measures."
}
